parts.title: Renting a Flat
parts.scenario: A young woman phones a letting agency to register as a tenant and hear about three flats that might suit her.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Daniel
voices.desc: Letting agent — male, 30s, upbeat, professional, slightly salesy; British accent

voices.label: Megan
voices.desc: Caller — female, early 20s, friendly, a little nervous at first, then decisive; British accent

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a young woman phoning a letting agency about renting a flat. First, you have some time to look at Questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [telephone rings twice, then the line clicks open] [bright, professional] Good morning, Calder Lettings, Daniel speaking. How can I help?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [a little nervous, friendly] Oh, hi. Um, I filled in the form on your website last week about renting a one-bedroom flat, but nobody's got back to me, so I thought I'd just ring.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [apologetic] Ah, sorry about that, we've had a bit of a backlog. [practical] Let me take your details again and I'll set you up properly on our system. Can I have your name?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: It's Megan Rennison.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [typing, murmuring] Megan... and that's R... E... N... I... S... O... N?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [correcting him politely] Nearly. Rennison has a double N. So R... E... double N... I... S... O... N.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [reading it back carefully] Double N. Got it, thanks. And what do you do, Megan? The landlords always ask about employment.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [light laugh] Sure. Well, until the spring I was a receptionist at a dental surgery, and people still assume I'm a dental nurse, but I've actually just qualified as a paramedic. [quietly proud] I started with the ambulance service in May.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [impressed] Oh, well done. [brisk] And when are you hoping to move in?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [thinking aloud] So, my current tenancy ends on the thirty-first of July, but I don't want to rush into anything, so I'll stay with my sister for a bit. Um... she's away herself until the middle of August, so... [decisive] I'd say from the twenty-third of August. Not before that.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [noting it down] The twenty-third. That's good timing, actually. A lot of our flats come free around then. Now, what's your budget per month?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [hesitant] Well, on the online form I put nine hundred pounds...

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [knowing] Mm-hm.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [sighs] ...but I've been looking around, and I don't think I'll find anything decent for that. So I could stretch to nine hundred and fifty. [firm] I really can't go any higher than that, though.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [reassuring] That's realistic for this area. Is that including bills?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: No, that's just the rent. I'll pay the bills on top.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [practical] Fine. Just so you know, there's a holding deposit of one week's rent when you apply, and then a full deposit of five weeks' rent before you move in. We'll also need a reference from your current landlord.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [relaxed] That's no problem. I've always paid on time, so she's happy to write one.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [businesslike] Great. And is there anything the landlord would need to agree to? Any special requirements?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [slightly anxious] Yes, er, I've got a pet. [quickly] Not a dog. Everyone assumes that. And it isn't a cat either, I know landlords worry about their carpets. It's a rabbit. She lives indoors, in a big cage.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [amused, chuckles] A rabbit. That shouldn't put most of them off, but I'll make a note so there are no surprises. [shifting to business] Right. I've got three flats on my list at the moment that might suit you. Shall I tell you about them?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [eager] Yes, please. Hang on, let me find a pen... OK, go ahead.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [clear, informative] OK. The first one's on Mill Lane, near the park. The rent is eight hundred and seventy-five a month, so that's well within your budget.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [pleased] Oh, nice. What floor is it on? I'd rather not be on the ground floor, to be honest.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [checking the screen] Well, the advert says second floor, but [correcting himself] actually, that's wrong. I went round there on Monday, and it's on the third floor. It's the top of the building, so it gets a lot of light.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [hopeful] That sounds lovely. Is there a catch?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [honest, slightly apologetic] The main thing is that there's no lift, so you'd be climbing three flights of stairs every day. [quickly, reassuring] Parking's fine, there's a residents' permit scheme, and the boiler was replaced last year.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [wry] Three flights with the shopping... and the rabbit's cage. Hmm. [short pause] OK, what's the second one?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [upbeat] That's on Carlton Road, just by the station. Nine hundred and thirty a month. It's been completely refurbished, so...

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [interrupting gently] Completely?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [qualifying, a little sheepish] Well... not quite. The bathroom wasn't touched, that's about ten years old, and the carpets are the same. But there's a brand-new kitchen, it was fitted just last month, and it's beautifully designed.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [interested] That's a big plus, I cook a lot. But is it noisy, being so close to the station?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [knowing] That's what everyone asks. [explaining] Actually, the trains aren't the issue, the windows are all double-glazed. The problem is that the flat is directly above a bakery, and they start work at about four in the morning. [chuckles] You'd wake up to the smell of fresh bread, but you'd also hear the ovens and the delivery vans.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [laughing] With my shifts, I'm sometimes up at four anyway. [thoughtful] And the third?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [measured] The third is in Orchard Court, the new development by the river. That's nine hundred and ninety, so a bit over...

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [firmly] Yes, that's more than I said I could pay.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [persuasive] I know, but it might be worth a look, because the landlord's said he may come down a little. It hasn't got a garden. There used to be a shared one, but it's been turned into car parking. But there's a really large balcony, big enough for a table and chairs, and it gets the sun all afternoon.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [tempted] Oh, I'd love some outdoor space. Is there any storage?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [informative] Plenty. Each flat has its own storeroom in the basement.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [deciding] OK. Could I see all three? Maybe Carlton Road first, because of the kitchen?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [pleased] Of course. I could do Thursday afternoon, say two o'clock, and then go straight on to the other two.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [apologetic] Ah, I'm on a late shift on Thursday. Friday morning would be better.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [checking] Friday at ten, then. I'll meet you outside the bakery, and I'll text you the details this afternoon.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: [warm] Perfect. Thanks so much, Daniel.

parts.title: A New Exhibition of Historical Maps
parts.context: Monologue in an everyday social context (1 speaker)
parts.scenario: A museum curator introduces a group of visitors to a new exhibition of historical maps and explains the layout of the gallery.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Curator
voices.desc: Museum curator — female, 50s, warm, articulate, enthusiastic with a dry sense of humour; British accent

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a museum curator talking to a group of visitors about a new exhibition. First, you have some time to look at Questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: Curator
script.text: [small gallery, voices settling] [warm, welcoming] Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the Harland Museum. My name's Ruth Calloway, and I'm the curator of our new exhibition, Lines on the Land, which brings together five centuries of maps. Before you go in, I'd like to tell you a little about how it came about, and how the gallery is laid out.

script.speaker: Curator
script.text: [conversational] A lot of people assume the exhibition was planned to celebrate the museum's two-hundredth anniversary. [light laugh] It wasn't. That's not until next year. And while we did receive a very generous gift of sea charts from the Whitlock family last spring, those had already been earmarked for a separate display.

script.speaker: Curator
script.text: [animated] The real starting point was rather more dramatic. Three years ago, builders were renovating the east wing, and behind some old wooden panelling they found a rolled-up estate map, almost perfectly preserved. [short pause] Everything you'll see today grew out of the questions that map raised.

script.speaker: Curator
script.text: [explaining] Now, most map exhibitions tell the story in date order, from the oldest to the newest, and we did consider doing that. In the end, though, we decided to group the maps according to what they were made for. So there are maps for war, maps for trade, maps for religious pilgrimage, and so on. [wry] It means a sixteenth-century chart can hang next to a twentieth-century one, which some visitors find a little disorienting at first.

script.speaker: Curator
script.text: [slightly regretful] We'd also hoped to have material from every continent, but sadly two of our loans, from Australia and from Brazil, fell through at the last minute, so the collection is more European than I'd have liked.

script.speaker: Curator
script.text: [enthusiastic] Let me mention one map in particular. The oldest piece in the show is a map of a river valley drawn by a monk called Brother Anselm. [clarifying] We're in the unusual position of knowing exactly who made it, because he wrote his name in the corner. You'll notice some water stains, and there's a popular story that it survived a flood at the abbey. In fact, the stains came from a leaking roof in a Victorian library, much more recently.

script.speaker: Curator
script.text: [lowering voice, as if sharing a secret] What's really exciting is that for decades it was catalogued as a fifteenth-century map. When we analysed the ink last year, it turned out to be nearly two hundred years older than anyone had thought.

script.speaker: Curator
script.text: [practical] I'd strongly suggest you pick up an audio guide at the desk. It isn't free, I'm afraid, there's a charge of three pounds. We'd planned to include interviews with descendants of some of the mapmakers, but that part hasn't been recorded yet. [warmly] What the guide does brilliantly, though, is decode all the little pictures and signs on the maps, which most of us simply can't read today.

script.speaker: Curator
script.text: [gently firm] Photography is allowed throughout, but please switch off your flash. Some of the inks are extremely sensitive to light, which is also why the gallery is kept rather dim. [light laugh] Your eyes will adjust after a minute or two, I promise.

script.speaker: Curator
script.text: [brisk] And a couple of changes since we first advertised the exhibition. We originally said you'd have to book tickets online in advance, but demand has been manageable, so you can just turn up. Children under twelve still pay a reduced price, by the way. They don't get in free. And the late opening, which was going to be on Thursdays, will now be on Fridays, until nine.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at Questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: Curator
script.text: [clear, guiding] Right, let me explain the layout. If you look at the plan in your leaflet, you'll see the entrance at the bottom, and as you come in, the ticket desk is immediately on your right.

script.speaker: Curator
script.text: [informative] Go past the desk and right into that corner, and you'll find the Whitlock sea charts. [explaining] You might expect them to be along the right-hand wall by the windows, but the light would fade the colours, so they're tucked away in the corner instead.

script.speaker: Curator
script.text: [enthusiastic] In the centre of the room, you can't miss the giant globe. [correcting an impression] The interactive map table was originally going to stand between the entrance and the globe, but it caused queues right at the door. So it's now on the far side of the globe, between the globe and the doorway to the shop.

script.speaker: Curator
script.text: [measured] Along the left-hand wall there are two large cases. The one nearest the entrance holds our Roman road maps. [emphatic] The estate map, the one the builders found, is in the second case along, halfway down that wall.

script.speaker: Curator
script.text: [guiding] In the top left-hand corner you'll see the staircase up to the library. There's a short film about how maps were engraved and printed, and that's shown on a screen just to the right of the stairs as you face them. [clarifying] Not underneath them. That space is only used for storage.

script.speaker: Curator
script.text: [slightly amused] Just to the left of the shop doorway is where the children's trail begins, and you'll probably hear it before you see it. And halfway along the window wall there's a row of benches, if you need a rest, with a lovely view of the river.

script.speaker: Curator
script.text: [informative] And finally, our replica printing press. We'd hoped to put it in the middle of the window wall, but the floor there isn't strong enough to take the weight. So it's in the top right-hand corner, to the right of the shop doorway. [warmly] Our volunteers give demonstrations every hour. [short pause] Right, do enjoy the exhibition, and do come and find me if you have any questions.

question_groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.prompt: What led to the idea for the exhibition?

options.A: an important date in the museum's history
options.B: a donation from a local family
options.C: an unexpected find in the building

items.evidence: behind some old wooden panelling they found a rolled-up estate map
items.trap: The anniversary (A) is denied ('It wasn't') and the Whitlock gift (B) was for a separate display.

items.prompt: According to the curator, what is unusual about the exhibition?

options.A: It is arranged by the function of the maps.
options.B: It includes maps from all over the world.
options.C: It follows a strict historical sequence.

items.evidence: we decided to group the maps according to what they were made for
items.trap: Date order (C) was considered and rejected; the loans from other continents (B) fell through.

items.prompt: What does the curator say about the map by Brother Anselm?

options.B: It was damaged during a flood.
options.C: Its age had been incorrectly recorded.

items.evidence: it turned out to be nearly two hundred years older than anyone had thought
items.trap: The maker's name is known (A is the reverse), and the flood story (B) is said to be untrue.

items.prompt: The curator recommends the audio guide because it
items.evidence: decode all the little pictures and signs on the maps
items.trap: It isn't free (A), and the interviews with descendants (B) haven't been recorded yet.

items.prompt: What change has been made to the original arrangements?

options.A: Tickets must now be reserved beforehand.
options.B: The museum stays open late on a different day.
options.C: Young children no longer have to pay.

items.evidence: which was going to be on Thursdays, will now be on Fridays
items.trap: Advance booking (A) was the original plan, now dropped; children still pay a reduced price (C).

parts.title: A Presentation on Bioplastics
parts.context: Academic discussion: student and tutor (2 speakers)
parts.scenario: An environmental science student discusses a draft of his presentation on bioplastics with his tutor.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Dr Hollis
voices.desc: Tutor — female, 50s, incisive, dry humour, encouraging but frank; British accent

voices.label: Liam
voices.desc: Student — male, early 20s, relaxed, enthusiastic, quick to concede a point; Australian accent

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear a student called Liam talking to his tutor about a presentation he is preparing on bioplastics. First, you have some time to look at Questions 21 to 26.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [a knock, a door opening] [warm, brisk] Come in, Liam, have a seat. So, the bioplastics presentation. How's it coming along?

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [relaxed, slightly rueful] Yeah, not bad. I've got a full draft, but I wanted to run through the section on the different sources with you before I finalise the slides.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [encouraging] Good idea. Go on, then.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [explaining] So I start with corn starch, because it's still the most widely used. And I'd written that the big problem with it is that it's brittle, you know, it cracks easily...

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [doubtful] Hmm, I'd be careful there. That was true of the early versions, but the blends they use now are surprisingly tough. And you've got a line here about toxic by-products. I couldn't find any reliable source for that.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [conceding, a little embarrassed] Fair enough, I think I got that off a blog. [thinking aloud] So really it comes down to the fact that every hectare of maize grown for plastic is a hectare that isn't feeding anyone.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [firmly] Exactly. That's the argument you should lead with.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [moving on] Then sugarcane. Now, I went in thinking this was the worst of the lot, because you hear so much about rainforest being cleared for plantations.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [measured] And?

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [animated] Well, the more I read, the more I realised that's mostly a myth, at least where plastics are concerned. Most of it's made from bagasse, the fibre that's left over once the sugar's been extracted, so it doesn't need any extra land at all. [emphatic] I reckon it gets a lot of stick that it really doesn't deserve.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [approving] I'd go along with that. And it's cheap to process, which helps.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [enthusiastic] Seaweed's my favourite, honestly. I assumed supply would be the sticking point, since wild seaweed can only be harvested at certain times...

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [interjecting] But it's farmed now, isn't it? All year round.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: Yeah, exactly, so that's not an issue. And it's strong enough for most packaging. [sighs] The trouble is, it still costs about four times as much to make as ordinary plastic, and until that comes down, no manufacturer's going to touch it.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [dry] Sadly, I think you're right.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [amused] Then there's the one made from used cooking oil, collected from restaurants.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [chuckles] Ah yes. I find that one rather appealing. The oil's a waste product, so it ought to be cheap.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: It is, the cost's fine. But the bags they trialled apparently kept a faint whiff of chips, [laughs] which isn't ideal if you're wrapping, I don't know, a birthday cake.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [laughing] No, quite. Make sure you mention that.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [more serious] Next is chitosan, which comes from shrimp and crab shells. People expect it to smell of fish...

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [sceptical] And doesn't it?

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [firm] No, it's completely odourless once it's been processed. And it's tough. The problem is that the shells only come in while the fishing season's open, so for months on end there's nothing to work with.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [thoughtful] So the factories would be sitting idle half the year. Yes, that's a real limitation.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [wrapping up the list] And the last one is potato peel, from crisp factories.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [interested] I'd have thought the supply there was enormous.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: It is. They run all year, so there's no shortage, and it isn't expensive either. But the material just doesn't hold up. It tears really easily, so you couldn't use it for anything heavier than, say, a sandwich wrapper.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [agreeing] That's fair. Just make that point clearly. [short pause] Oh, and one more thing before we move on. Are you going to explain the difference between biodegradable and compostable? Because a lot of your audience will assume they're the same.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [a bit caught out] Ah. I hadn't planned to, no. I suppose I could add a slide near the start, saying that compostable means it breaks down within a set time, but usually only in an industrial facility, not a garden heap.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [approving] Yes, do. Otherwise half your argument won't make sense to them.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 27 to 30.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [curious] Remind me, what made you pick this topic in the first place? Was it your summer job?

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [laughs] At the packaging firm in Brisbane? No, I was only stacking boxes there, I never saw how anything was made. And I'd actually put down ocean plastics as my first choice, and nobody else had chosen it, so I could easily have kept it. [reflective] It was a documentary about compostable coffee cups that changed my mind. I watched it one night and just couldn't stop thinking about it.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [practical] Well, it shows. Now, the slides. You've got twelve for fifteen minutes, which is about right, so don't worry about the number.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [uncertain] I was worried I'd crammed too much writing onto them.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [reassuring] Actually, no, you've been quite disciplined, it's mostly key words. [frank] My concern is the graphs. The labels are tiny and the colours are almost identical, so from the back of a lecture theatre no one will be able to make them out.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [rueful] Right. I'll redo those. [hesitant] And for the opening, I was going to hit them with a statistic, like how many million tonnes of plastic get made every year.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [doubtful] Everyone does that, and the numbers are so huge they don't mean anything to people.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [trying again] Or I could put a question to the audience. Like, who here has used a compostable cup this week?

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [cautious] That can fall rather flat if nobody answers. [warming up] What about the thing you told me last week? When you buried a so-called biodegradable cup in your garden and dug it up six months later?

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [laughing] And it looked brand new.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [decisive] Exactly. Start there. It happened to you, it's memorable, and it leads straight into your argument.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [convinced] OK, yeah, I'll do that. And the conclusion? I wondered whether it's a bit short.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [considering] Short is no bad thing at the end. And you haven't brought in any new material, which is good, because people often do. [frank] But you never actually tell us what you think should happen. You list the pros and cons, and then you just stop.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [sighs] So I'm sitting on the fence.

script.speaker: Dr Hollis
script.text: [dry, amused] Firmly. Give them a clear recommendation, even if it's a cautious one.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: [decisive] Right. I'll argue that seaweed deserves the research funding. That's what I actually believe, anyway.

parts.title: The Domestication of the Horse
parts.scenario: An archaeology lecturer explains how new evidence has changed ideas about where and when the horse was domesticated.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Lecturer
voices.desc: University lecturer — male, 40s, clear, engaging, precise, occasionally wry; British accent

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about the domestication of the horse. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [lecture theatre, faint murmur fading] [clear, engaging] Good morning. Today I want to look at one of the most consequential partnerships in human history, the one between people and horses. [measured] It's a story that has been substantially rewritten in the last decade or so, largely thanks to genetics, so some of what you'll find in older textbooks is, frankly, out of date. [brisk] I'll start with the evidence that was traditionally used, then turn to what the DNA tells us, and finish with how the horse spread.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] For a long time, the strongest candidate for the first horse-keeping society was the Botai culture, in what is now northern Kazakhstan, around three thousand five hundred BCE. The Botai were clearly obsessed with horses. At some of their settlements, horse bones make up more than ninety per cent of all the animal remains.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [explaining carefully] Of course, huge numbers of bones might simply mean very successful hunting. So researchers looked for evidence that the animals were controlled. The first line of evidence came not from the legs or the spine, where you might expect to see signs of heavy work, but from the teeth. Some Botai horses had small areas of wear on their premolars, which was interpreted as damage from a bit, the piece of equipment placed in a horse's mouth to steer it.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [animated] The second line of evidence was chemical. Researchers analysed residues left inside Botai pottery. [emphasising the contrast] Now, if these people were hunters, you'd expect fats from horse meat, and that wasn't what made the headlines. What was significant was the presence of fats from mare's milk. [short pause] And you can't milk a wild horse, or at least, not twice.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured] Thirdly, there's the question of whether horses were kept in enclosures. Excavators had found rings of post holes, but these were ambiguous, as they could equally be the remains of houses. Much more persuasive were unusually high levels of nitrogen and phosphorus in the soil within certain areas, which is what you'd get from large quantities of dung accumulating in a pen.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [pivoting, more serious] So the case for Botai looked strong. Then, in two thousand and eighteen, a genetic study sequenced the DNA of Botai horses, and the results were a real surprise. They were not the ancestors of the horses we ride today. Instead, they were the ancestors of the Przewalski "/ʃəˈvælski/" horse, the stocky animal found on the Mongolian steppe.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [wry] This had an awkward consequence. Przewalski's horse had always been celebrated as the last truly wild horse on Earth. [firm] That description can no longer stand. If its ancestors were kept by the Botai, then Przewalski's horses are feral, that is, descended from domesticated animals that escaped human control and returned to life in the wild. [aside] Incidentally, by the late nineteen-sixties they had disappeared from the wild altogether, and every one alive today is descended from a handful of animals kept in zoos.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [thoughtful] That left an obvious question. If modern domestic horses didn't come from Botai, where did they come from? Over the years, various regions had been proposed, including Anatolia, in modern Turkey, and the Iberian Peninsula. [clear, deliberate] A very large study published in two thousand and twenty-one, which analysed the genomes of hundreds of ancient horses, finally gave an answer: the western steppe, around the lower reaches of the Volga and Don rivers, in what is now southern Russia, at roughly two thousand two hundred BCE.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [engaged] The same study identified genes that seem to have been strongly selected by those early breeders. You might expect speed to have been a priority. [short pause] It wasn't, at least not at first. One of the genes is associated with a stronger back, which would have made the animals better able to carry riders and loads.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [explaining] Another is linked to more docile behaviour. Wild horses are prey animals and they panic easily. An animal that was less fearful, and therefore less likely to bolt or kick, would have been far more valuable to its owners than one that was simply bigger or faster.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured, building the argument] There's a further clue in how quickly generations succeeded each other. Around this time, the average interval between a horse's birth and the birth of its offspring fell to roughly half its previous length. [emphatic] This isn't something that happens naturally. It only really makes sense if people were deliberately controlling breeding, choosing which animals mated, and when.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [turning to a new point] Now, the genetic evidence has also forced us to revisit the role of the Yamnaya people, who spread from the steppe into Europe from about three thousand BCE. [slightly ironic] There's a dramatic image, which you'll still find in popular books, of Yamnaya warriors galloping westwards on horseback.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [firm] Unfortunately for that picture, the horses found at the relevant sites don't belong to the modern domestic lineage at all. [explaining] What seems to have made the Yamnaya so mobile was not riding, but heavy wagons, drawn by oxen, which allowed whole families to move with their possessions.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [picking up pace, animated] Once the modern domestic horse had emerged, though, it spread extraordinarily fast, reaching Anatolia, central Europe and much of Asia within a few centuries after two thousand BCE. What drove that expansion? Not cavalry. Mounted warfare on any real scale comes considerably later. [emphatic] The key development was the chariot, a light, fast vehicle with spoked wheels, which turned the horse into a weapon of enormous prestige.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [reflective, winding up] So, to sum up. The Botai story isn't wrong, exactly, because the Botai clearly did manage horses in some way. But they turned out to be a side branch rather than the main trunk of the family tree. [wry] It's a useful reminder that archaeological evidence which seems to point clearly in one direction can be overturned very quickly by a new technique. [brisk] Next week, we'll look at what happened when horses reached the Americas.
